**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination / Technical and Vocational Education Examination. Economics 2 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FIVE questions, choosing AT LEAST TWO from each section. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: La consigne « Answer FIVE questions, choosing AT LEAST TWO from each section » (5 questions en tout, au moins 2 par section) n'est pas exprimable dans regles_choix : chaque section porte la règle « répondre à 2 sur 4 » (le minimum imposé) et la consigne complète figure dans introduction_markdown.
Le sujet est un scan sans corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées ; les chiffres des exemples sont hypothétiques (aucune statistique réelle).

Question 4 : le sujet imprime « Discuss the: (a) advantages and (b) disadvantages of the government instituting a minimum wage legislation » avec « (10 +10 marks) » ; les points sont 10 pour (a) et 10 pour (b). Le diagramme du salaire minimum est décrit dans le corrigé, sans PNG.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Discuss the:

(a) advantages of the government instituting a minimum wage legislation.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A minimum wage law fixes by law the **lowest wage** that an employer may pay for an hour, a day or a month of work (in Cameroon there is a guaranteed minimum wage, the SMIG). It is a price floor in the labour market, set above the wage that would otherwise be paid to the lowest-paid workers. The main advantages are as follows.

1. **Reduces poverty and raises the income of the low paid.** Workers in the lowest-paid jobs earn more, so they can afford food, housing, health care and school fees; this raises their standard of living.
2. **Reduces exploitation.** Where employers have strong bargaining power (a few employers in a region, many unskilled job-seekers, workers without trade-union protection), wages may be pushed below the value of the worker's contribution; the minimum wage protects workers against such **monopsony power**.
3. **Reduces income inequality.** It narrows the gap between high and low earners and so contributes to social justice.
4. **Raises productivity and motivation.** Better-paid workers are better fed, healthier and more committed; the cost of recruiting and training is reduced because there is less labour turnover and absenteeism (the *efficiency wage* argument).
5. **Increases the incentive to work.** A higher wage makes employment more attractive than unemployment, begging or informal work, and so increases the supply of labour to the formal sector.
6. **Raises aggregate demand.** Low-income earners spend nearly all of any extra income on locally produced goods and services (high marginal propensity to consume), so the demand for local products rises and this may increase output and employment.
7. **Reduces government spending on welfare and increases tax revenue.** Higher wages mean fewer people needing public help and more income and sales tax collected.
8. **Prevents unfair competition between firms.** Firms cannot gain an advantage simply by paying lower wages than their rivals, so competition is based on efficiency and quality; the law also stops employers from cutting wages in a recession.
9. **Encourages employers to invest in training and in better technology**, to make workers more productive and worth their pay.

**Evaluation.** The benefits are greatest when the minimum wage is set **close to the market wage** and is **enforced**; for workers who are employed in the formal sector it gives real protection, and the gain in income may offset the possible fall in employment.

**Conclusion.** The main advantages are higher incomes for the low paid, protection against exploitation, less inequality and higher productivity and demand.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Discuss the:

(b) disadvantages of the government instituting a minimum wage legislation.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A minimum wage fixed by law above the equilibrium wage is a **price floor** in the labour market. Its main disadvantages are the following.

**Diagram (how to draw it).** Put the wage on the vertical axis and the quantity of labour on the horizontal axis. Draw a downward-sloping demand curve for labour (D) and an upward-sloping supply curve (S) that meet at the equilibrium wage $W_e$ and the employment level $L_e$. Draw a horizontal line at the legal minimum wage $W_{min}$ **above** $W_e$. At $W_{min}$ employers want only $L_d$ workers (less than $L_e$) while $L_s$ workers want to work (more than $L_e$): the horizontal gap between $L_s$ and $L_d$ is **surplus labour, that is unemployment**.

1. **Unemployment.** The higher cost of labour makes employers hire fewer workers (the quantity of labour demanded falls) while more people seek work; the unemployment is greatest for **young, unskilled and inexperienced workers**, whose productivity is lower than the legal minimum. The more elastic the demand for labour, the larger the loss of jobs.
2. **Higher production costs and higher prices.** Wage costs rise, and firms pass them on to consumers: **cost-push inflation**, which reduces the real value of the higher wage and may start a wage-price spiral.
3. **Reduced profits, investment and competitiveness.** Small firms with low profit margins may cut investment, close down or move to places without the law; exports become less competitive abroad.
4. **Substitution of capital for labour.** Firms replace workers with machines, which reduces employment in labour-intensive sectors.
5. **Growth of the informal sector and evasion.** In developing countries a large part of the workforce is employed in the informal sector or in subsistence agriculture, where the law does not apply or cannot be enforced; firms may pay workers under the table, so the law helps only a minority and the workers who lose formal jobs move to the informal sector, increasing its size and keeping wages there low.
6. **Costly to enforce.** The government needs labour inspectors and courts, which is expensive; it also has to revise the wage regularly or it becomes outdated (too high in a recession, too low in a boom).
7. **Poor targeting.** Some low-wage workers may be members of households that are not poor (students, secondary earners), while the poorest, who are unemployed, gain nothing; a tax credit or a subsidy may be a better way to help the poor.
8. **Distortion of market signals.** A uniform national wage ignores differences in the cost of living and productivity between regions and sectors, and may prevent the market from allocating labour efficiently.
9. **Fall in the quality of jobs.** Employers may reduce training, fringe benefits or working hours in order to offset the higher wage.

**Evaluation.** The size of the harm depends on **how far the minimum is above the equilibrium wage**, on the **elasticity of demand for labour**, on the strength of the economy (in a boom, little unemployment is created) and on whether employers have monopsony power (in which case a moderate minimum wage can even raise employment).

**Conclusion.** A minimum wage law can create unemployment, raise prices, hurt small firms and stay ineffective in the informal sector; for these reasons the level has to be set with care and with other policies, such as training and job creation.
